title: Pattern Strip
description: Find the group that repeats, or the move made at every step, and carry a picture pattern on until it comes round again.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: again, sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one pill per phase across bar, pitch 158; in user mode each is a button with a 72-tall finger box

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Find the group that repeats, or the move made at every step, and carry a picture pattern on until it comes round to the start again.
writeup.look: A long strip of cells with the last few empty, a turn dial under it, and a ring of numbered places at one side of the stage.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Pattern Strip' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the places filled against the places this phase leaves empty, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each cell or each place on the order line fills, and the second is fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The strip runs across the top of the working area: ten cells, each 100 by 100 with 8 between, at 64,222, reaching 1136. Each cell holds one shape, one arrow, or one dot on a plus-shaped outline, drawn at one size and never overlapping its neighbour. The bracket rides a rail under the strip, 1072 by 24 at 64,330, and is dragged to cover any run of cells. Copy light then lights every copy of that run along the whole strip at once, each matching copy underlined in green. A copy that does not match is left unlit, never hidden, and the one cell in it that breaks the match is ringed in reddish purple. The side count row runs under the rail, 1072 by 36 at 64,362, writing each shape's number of straight sides under its cell. The lower band, from 414 to 720, holds the dial on the first three phases. The dial is 160 across and docks under whichever empty cell is being filled, kept inside the working area's right edge, with the turn ring 72 across at its left. Each tap turns the dial's arrow one quarter turn clockwise, the way a clock's hands go, and draws that turn as a vermilion arc. The turn ring fills one quarter at a time and closes at four, when the arrow is home. On the fourth phase the dial is parked and the lower band holds the ring bay instead. The ring is 280 across at 64,420, with up to eight numbered places evenly round it. With two rings on, a second ring of the same size stands at 364,420 and reads the same draw. The draw drum is 120 by 120 at 664,420, and the order line is 440 by 80 at 664,620. The order line fills place by place as the order is read off the ring, and a vermilion arc joins the last number back to the first. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is a shape tray of the cells this strip uses and a turn pad of four arrows, pointing up, right, down and left. Twelve number keys three across take over wherever a count or an order is asked for. A word pad carries this strip's own words: group, repeat, quarter turn, clockwise, sides, first and last. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Whatever the stage hands over is deep blue: a given term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter, a tile already laid. The first member of a repeating group is deep blue too, and the second member, or a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself is vermilion in every tool without exception: a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, an operation sign, a key's shift. Whatever the rule makes is green: a next term, a built box, a coded or decoded letter, a copy just laid, a tick. Whatever the child is asked to notice is reddish purple: a broken box, a closed-in gap, a doubled part, a leftover counter, a line put back. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome. Chrome never borrows a content colour, and no content colour is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a thing is told by its label or its place before it is told by its colour. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. An order is never drawn as a line with two ends until it has been read off the ring. A line with ends is exactly the picture that stops at the last number, so the ring comes first and the line is only ever a copy of a walk round it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the strip the child finished, its repeating group bracketed and every copy lit, and the ring with the order they read off it.

phases.win: every copy of the group lights along the strip and the blanks fill with the matching shapes
phases.does: draws a bracket over the group they think repeats, watches its copies light, then fills the blanks
phases.goal: the smallest group that repeats fills every blank in a row
phases.says: Which shapes come round again? Put a bracket over them.
phases.check: Away from the screen: make a row of three kinds of thing on your desk. Ask a friend to find the group.
phases.feels: the row is one group laid down again and again, and a blank is only the next place in the group
phases.hands: Before the tool is opened, make a row on a desk with real things: square, square, circle, square, square, circle, in paper cut-outs, caps or beads. Ask for the smallest group that repeats, not for the next thing. Every row of the recap's matching question takes turns between two shapes, so give a group of three early, where copying two places back goes wrong. Let the class find where it breaks, and then ask how a group could be checked without filling any blank at all.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which cells come round again? Second rung, the phase's: does every copy of your group match? Third rung: the strip is cut to two whole copies of the group and one blank, and the child brackets again. The shape tray stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: every row of the recap's matching question takes turns between two shapes, so copying two places back has been right four times running.
wrong.move: copies the cell two places back into every blank, which works while two shapes take turns and finds no group at all.
wrong.screen: the child's shapes stay in the blanks, and a bracket is drawn over the two cells they were copied from. Copy light runs that pair along the strip. On a group of three the copies stop matching at the third cell, which is left unlit and ringed in reddish purple. A bracket over three cells is then offered beside it, and every copy of that one lights.

wrong.why: a longer bracket seems safer, because it holds more of the row inside it.
wrong.move: brackets a run one cell too long, taking in the start of the next copy, and fills the blank from it.
wrong.screen: copy light runs the long bracket along the strip, and each copy drifts one cell further until one does not match. That copy is left unlit with its breaking cell ringed. The child's bracket stays drawn, and it is then shortened one cell at a time, with the copies lit again after each.

phases.screen: a strip of shapes with its last two cells empty and the bracket waiting
phases.soWhat: Find the smallest group that repeats, and every blank takes the cell one whole group before it.

phases.win: the arrow settles and the turn ring closes when four quarter turns bring it home
phases.does: turns the dial until the new arrow repeats the move between the cells before it
phases.goal: the same quarter turn is made at every step, and four of them make a full turn
phases.says: How far did it turn each time? Make the same turn again.
phases.check: Point an arrow up and turn it a quarter turn clockwise three times. Which way does it point now?
phases.feels: the same small turn every time, and after four of them the arrow is back where it began
phases.hands: Give each pair a paper arrow and lay it flat on the desk pointing left. Turn it a quarter turn the way a clock's hands go, and say the new direction aloud. Keep turning and counting until the arrow comes home. Then ask how many turns brought it home, and which way it will point after eight turns, before anyone turns it.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how far did the arrow turn between the last two cells? Second rung, the phase's: which way do a clock's hands go? Third rung: the row is cut to two arrows one quarter turn apart, and the child makes the same turn once. The turn pad stays open.

wrong.why: a quarter turn is the same size either way, and the row shows only where the arrow pointed, not which way it moved between cells.
wrong.move: turns the arrow against a clock's hands, so a row that went up, right, down is carried on the other way round.
wrong.screen: the dial replays the move between the last two cells one quarter at a time, drawing it as a vermilion arc the way a clock's hands go. The child's arrow stays in its cell with its own arc drawn beside it, running the other way. The two arcs stand together, and nothing is marked.

wrong.why: a half turn is the easiest turn to see, because the arrow ends up pointing straight back the way it came.
wrong.move: makes a half turn at every step, so up is followed by down and the arrow never points right or left.
wrong.screen: the turn ring shows the child's move as two quarters filled, where the row made one. The dial then turns from the last cell one quarter at a time, and the arrow lands on a direction the child's row skipped. The child's arrow and the dial's stand side by side.

phases.screen: a row of arrows, each pointing a different way, with the dial under the first empty cell
phases.soWhat: A turning pattern makes the same quarter turn at every step, and four quarter turns make a full turn.
phases.concept: A quarter turn at every step

phases.win: the next shape lands and its count starts the row of numbers again from the top
phases.does: reads the side counts, then chooses the shape for the empty cell
phases.goal: a row can lose one side at each step and then start again from its first shape
phases.says: Count the sides of each one. What happens after three?
phases.check: A row starts with a shape of five sides and loses one each step. Name the shapes until it starts again.
phases.feels: the counts go down one at a time until they cannot go any lower, and then the row starts over
phases.hands: Draw a hexagon, a pentagon, a square and a triangle on the board, and count the sides of each aloud with the class. Ask what shape would have two sides, and let someone try to draw one that closes. Then ask where the row must go after the triangle. Write the side counts under the shapes, so the class sees a list of numbers that starts again.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many sides has the last shape? Second rung, the phase's: can a closed shape with straight sides have fewer than three? Third rung: the row is cut to a square, a triangle and one empty cell, with the row's first shape shown at the left. The shape tray stays open.

wrong.why: the row has lost one side at every step so far, and nothing on the strip says the losing has to stop.
wrong.move: looks for a shape with two sides after the triangle, and draws two straight lines meeting at a point.
wrong.screen: the child's two lines are drawn in the empty cell as they were made. The side counter writes two under them and rings the open end in reddish purple, where no side closes the shape. The strip then shows the row's first shape again after the triangle, and the counts under it start again from the top.

wrong.why: every step so far has been one side fewer, so a jump back up to the first count looks like the rule being broken.
wrong.move: reads the first shape coming back after the triangle as a slip in the row, and carries on losing sides.
wrong.screen: the bracket is drawn over the run from the first shape to the triangle, and copy light lights the second copy, starting at the shape that came back. The side counts under the row are drawn as two runs, the second starting under that shape. The child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a row of shapes with their side counts written under them and one cell empty
phases.soWhat: A row can lose one side at each step until the triangle, and then it starts again from its first shape.
phases.concept: One side fewer, then start again

phases.win: the line fills round the ring and an arc joins the last number back to the first
phases.does: draws the starting number, then reads the order off the ring into the line
phases.goal: an order that goes round comes back to the first number after the last
phases.says: Who goes first? Now go round. Who comes after the last one?
phases.check: Away from the screen: four friends take turns in number order, and three is drawn. Say the whole order.
phases.feels: the order has a start and no end, and the draw decides where the start is
phases.hands: Seat four children in a circle holding number cards one to four, and draw a card from a bag. That number goes first, and the group says the whole order aloud going round. Draw again for a new event and say the order again. Then seat a second group of four beside the first and ask whether it needs a draw of its own. Name nobody; call each child by their number.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number was drawn? Second rung, the phase's: who comes after the last number? Third rung: the ring is cut to three places with the draw already made, and the child reads it round once. The number keys stay open.

wrong.why: a list of numbers has always stopped at its biggest number, and nothing on a written line says it carries on.
wrong.move: stops the order at the last number, leaving out every player whose number comes before the one drawn.
wrong.screen: the order line keeps the child's numbers and draws the places still to fill as empty outlined boxes. The ring is then walked from the drawn place, each number lighting as it is passed. The walk goes past the last number and on round to the first, and the arc joining them is drawn in vermilion.

wrong.why: the drawn number has to go first, and counting order is the only other order the class has ever used.
wrong.move: writes the drawn number first and then the rest in counting order from one, so a draw of four out of five gives four, one, two, three, five.
wrong.screen: the ring is walked from the drawn place, and each player's neighbour on the ring is lit beside them. The child's line stands under the order the ring gives. The one place where a neighbour changed, four and then one, is ringed in reddish purple.

wrong.why: each team has its own column to fill, and a new column looks as though it needs a new draw.
wrong.move: makes a new draw for the second team, so the two teams start from different numbers in one event.
wrong.screen: two rings stand side by side and read one draw together, and both order lines fill from the same start. The child's second order stays beside its ring, and the drum shows the single number drawn for the event.

phases.screen: numbered places round a ring, with the draw waiting and an empty order line beside it
phases.soWhat: In an order that goes round, whoever is drawn goes first, and after the last number comes the first again.
phases.concept: After the last comes the first

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when the last place of the order line fills. The line lifts off and bends itself round into a ring, and its two ends meet, so the last number sits beside the first. The drawn start carries a small flag. Drag the flag to any other number and the ring unrolls into a new line from there, with every neighbour kept. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked either way, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a strip of shapes stands with its last two cells empty and the bracket parked at its left hand end. On the second a row of arrows stands, each pointing a different way, with the dial docked under the first empty cell and its turn ring open. On the third a row of shapes stands with its side counts already written under it and one cell empty. On the fourth the ring bay is open with its numbered places drawn round it, the draw waiting and the order line empty. The running count at the top left holds the places filled against the places this phase leaves empty, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the parked bracket, or the dial, or the empty cell, or the draw, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what comes round again. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any strip of shapes, arrows or dots, any row of shapes, and any ring of up to eight numbered places, with the bracket, the dial, the side counter and the draw all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the group that repeats, a quarter turn at every step, a row that loses a side and starts again, and an order that goes round from a drawn start.
voiceLines: A strip of shapes, and some cells still empty. Find what comes round again.
Which shapes come round again? Put a bracket over them.
How far did it turn each time? Make the same turn again.
Count the sides of each one. What happens after three?
Who goes first? Now go round. Who comes after the last one?
Another row. Find the rule before you fill anything.
Free play. Any strip, any ring, with the bracket, the dial and the draw open.
Look again at what stays the same from one cell to the next.
Every row carried on, and every order brought round to its start.

observations.why: A group one cell too long or too short does not start again at the same place each time, so its copies drift.
observations.soWhat: The group that repeats is found by testing it along the whole row, not by looking at the last two cells.
observations.observe: The copies lit all along the strip only when the bracket covered the smallest group that repeats.

observations.why: Each quarter turn points the arrow a new way, and there are only four ways for it to point.
observations.soWhat: A turning pattern repeats every four steps, so a far step is found by counting in fours.
observations.observe: Four quarter turns closed the ring and brought the arrow back to where it began.

observations.why: A closed shape with straight sides needs at least three, so the row cannot lose another side.
observations.soWhat: Starting again is part of the pattern, so the group runs from the first shape to the triangle.
observations.observe: The side counts went down to three and then went back to the first count.

observations.why: Each player keeps the same neighbour wherever the order starts, so the order has a start but no end.
observations.soWhat: After the last number comes the first, and one draw sets the start for both teams.
observations.observe: The order line bent round into a ring, and the last number sat beside the first.

phases.screen: a strip of shapes with its last two cells empty and the bracket waiting
phases.win: every copy of the group lights along the strip and the blanks fill with the matching shapes
phases.traceback: Every copy of the child's run is lit along the strip and the cell that breaks a copy is ringed; then the smallest group is bracketed, its copies light and the blanks fill.
ladder: Read the beads along until the first colour comes back.
Name the shapes aloud and stop where the first one returns.
One shape may come more than once inside a group.
Does every copy of your group match?
Start at the first cell and stop where the row begins again.

phases.screen: a row of arrows, each pointing a different way, with the dial under the first empty cell
phases.win: the arrow settles and the turn ring closes when four quarter turns bring it home
phases.traceback: The dial replays the turn between the last two cells as a clockwise arc, quarter by quarter, and a ghost row under the strip ends on the arrow the rule makes.
ladder: Put your thumb on the arrow before the empty cell and turn it.
The dot steps to the next arm of the plus, no further.
Fill every cell, and watch the ring close each time.
Which way do the hands of a clock go?
Count the quarter turns between two arrows you can see.

phases.screen: a row of shapes with their side counts written under them and one cell empty
phases.win: the next shape lands and its count starts the row of numbers again from the top
phases.traceback: The child's figure is redrawn with its open end ringed, then the row's own counts are read out under it and the shape the rule makes lands in the cell.
ladder: Read the counts again and do the same to the last one.
Do the counts fall here, or do they climb?
Count the shapes you laid before the first one came back.
Can a closed shape with straight sides have fewer than three?
Say the side counts out loud, from the row's start.

phases.screen: numbered places round a ring, with the draw waiting and an empty order line beside it
phases.win: the line fills round the ring and an arc joins the last number back to the first
phases.traceback: The places still to fill are drawn as empty boxes, the ring is walked from the drawn place past the last number and on to the first, and an arc joins them.
ladder: The ring does not stop at the last place. Keep walking.
Each player keeps the same neighbour, wherever the order starts.
The one who goes last still has a neighbour after them.
Who comes after the last number?
On a ring there is no end. Keep walking round to the start.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: Every copy of the child's run is lit along the strip and the cell that breaks a copy is ringed; then the smallest group is bracketed, its copies light and the blanks fill.
Phase 2: The dial replays the turn between the last two cells as a clockwise arc, quarter by quarter, and a ghost row under the strip ends on the arrow the rule makes.
Phase 3: The child's figure is redrawn with its open end ringed, then the row's own counts are read out under it and the shape the rule makes lands in the cell.
Phase 4: The places still to fill are drawn as empty boxes, the ring is walked from the drawn place past the last number and on to the first, and an arc joins them.

voice.opening: A strip of shapes, with its last cells still empty. Find the rule and carry it on.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every row carried on, and every order brought round to its start.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: A bead string goes red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, and then two empty places. Which beads go in the two places?

question.en: These beads keep one group going. How many cells long is that group?

ask.en: How many cells in the group?

items.planQuestion: Star, moon, star, moon, star, and then an empty place. What goes in the empty place?

question.en: Star and moon, over and over again. Where does the group end?

items.planAnswer: Moon, because star and moon take turns

items.planQuestion: Square, square, circle, square, square, circle, square, and then an empty place. What goes there, and what is the group that repeats?

question.en: This strip hides a longer group. Where does it come round again?

items.planAnswer: Square, and the group is square, square, circle

items.planQuestion: An arrow points left. At every step it makes a quarter turn clockwise. Which way does it point after one, two, three and four steps?

question.en: Look at the turn from one cell to the next. Which way does the last arrow point?

items.planAnswer: Up, then right, then down, then left again

items.planQuestion: A dot sits at the bottom of a plus shape, then at the left, then at the top. It moves one place round clockwise each time. Where does it sit next?

question.en: Now a dot walks round a plus, one place at a time. Where does it sit next?

items.planQuestion: An arrow points down and makes a quarter turn clockwise at every step. Which way does it point after eight steps?

question.en: This arrow makes eight quarter turns, one for each cell. Where does it end?

items.planAnswer: Down again, because four quarter turns make a full turn and eight make two full turns

items.planQuestion: A row goes pentagon, square, triangle, pentagon, square, and then an empty place. Which shape goes there, and which comes after it?

question.en: Watch what the counts do along this row. Which shape belongs in the empty cell?

items.planAnswer: A triangle, and then a pentagon again

items.planQuestion: A row goes triangle, square, pentagon, triangle, square, and then an empty place. What goes in the empty place?

question.en: This row changes the other way. What must fill the cell now?

items.planAnswer: A pentagon, because the shapes gain one side each time, three, four, five, and then start again at three

items.planQuestion: A row starts with a seven-sided shape and loses one side at every step. How many shapes are in the row before it has to start again?

question.en: Lay each next shape with one side fewer. How many shapes until the row starts again?

items.planAnswer: Five: seven sides, six, five, four and three. A closed shape with straight sides needs at least three, so the row then starts again

items.planQuestion: Five children bat in turn in the order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, going round. Today a draw says child 4 bats first. Write the whole order.

question.en: Five children bat in turn, going round. Tap the drum to see who starts.

items.planQuestion: Two teams of five players take turns in the order of their numbers, going round, and one draw sets the start for both teams. The draw is 3. Write each team's order.

question.en: Two teams, one draw. Read the order for both teams off the ring.

items.planAnswer: 3, 4, 5, 1, 2 for both teams, because the same draw starts both

items.planQuestion: Six players take turns in the order 1 to 6, going round. Player 2 goes last. Who went first?

question.en: Six players take turns round the ring. This one goes last, so who went first?

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }
